name: Dermatofibroma
overview: Dermatofibroma is a common benign skin lesion composed of fibrous tissue within the dermis. These lesions often develop after minor skin trauma such as insect bites, small cuts, or folliculitis. They are non-cancerous, usually remain stable for many years, and rarely require treatment unless they become symptomatic or cosmetically bothersome.
description: Dermatofibromas typically present as firm, well-defined nodules that are fixed within the skin but movable over deeper tissues. They most commonly occur on the legs, especially in young and middle-aged adults, and are slightly more common in women. These lesions usually grow slowly before stabilizing and have an excellent long-term prognosis.
clinical_presentation: Brown, tan, pink, or reddish coloration
Most commonly located on the lower legs
Slow growth followed by long-term stability
typical_features: Diameter usually between 3 mm and 10 mm
Central dimpling when compressed from the sides
symptoms: Rare irritation from shaving or friction

ABCDE.Color: Uniform brown, tan, pink, or reddish

diagnostic_workup: Digital lesion photography if monitoring is required
Skin biopsy if diagnosis is uncertain or atypical features are present
treatment_options: No treatment required in most cases
Excision for cosmetic reasons after discussion with a dermatologist
prognosis: The prognosis is excellent. Dermatofibromas are benign lesions that do not metastasize. Most remain unchanged for many years, although slight enlargement may occasionally occur. Recurrence after complete surgical excision is uncommon.
prevention: There is no specific prevention strategy.
Prompt treatment of minor skin injuries may reduce local inflammation.
Routine skin self-examinations help identify new or changing lesions.
next_steps: Routine observation is appropriate for typical lesions.
Dermatology consultation is recommended if the diagnosis is uncertain.
Discuss surgical removal if the lesion becomes painful, repeatedly irritated, or cosmetically bothersome.
Seek medical evaluation if the lesion changes significantly in size, color, or shape.
red_flags: Loss of the typical dimple sign

follow_up.routine: Routine follow-up is generally unnecessary unless changes occur or recommended by your dermatologist.
follow_up.high_risk: Earlier dermatological evaluation is appropriate if rapid changes or atypical features develop.

patient_advice: Dermatofibromas are common benign skin lesions.
Avoid repeatedly scratching or traumatizing the lesion.
Monitor the lesion with occasional photographs.
Seek medical advice if rapid changes occur.
Continue routine skin self-examinations for other new lesions.
